Q: How can I prevent duplicate Celery tasks when a FastAPI endpoint is retried? A:

Since you're already have Redis (or valkey) in your stack, you can use its atomic operations to avoid race conditions.

Specifically, SET <key> <val> NX. The NX option is: "Only set the key if it does not already exist." Docs for redis-py set(). This will return Null, or None in Python, if the key already existed and was not set by that command.

If two different requests arrive simultaneously (or to different app instances), then the actual first one will get a True result and the other will get None. Use that as the check to determine if you should create the job or not. (Add additional logic for what to do when the job already exists or is not complete, etc., like showing the current status or progress.)

Note that I'm using explicit is None and is not None checks to avoid issues with False-like values.

The simplified pattern is:

result = redis_conn.set("some_key", "some_value", nx=True)  # the NX is important
if result is None:
    # the key already existed
    return current_job_id

# the key did not exist, so create a job, set the key in redis and return it
job = ProcessingJob(...)  # and commit
redis_conn.set("some_key", job.id, nx=True)
return job.id


# in the celery task, remove the redis key at the end
def process_report_task(job_id: int):
    # do all the task actions and then delete the key at the end
    redis_conn.delete("some_key")

Applying that to your code:

import redis

# this could in config, with connection pools and as FastAPI Dependency
redis_conn = redis.Redis(...)

@app.post("/reports/{report_id}/process")
async def process_report(report_id: int, db: Session = Depends(get_db)):
    job_key = f"process_report:{report_id}"
    # use a dummy value initially
    res = redis_conn.set(job_key, -1, nx=True)
    
    if res is None:
        # job already exists, get the current job from the DB and return that
        existing = (
            db.query(ProcessingJob)
            .filter(
                ProcessingJob.report_id == report_id,
                ProcessingJob.status.in_(["queued", "running"])
            )
            .first()
        )
        return {"job_id": existing.id}
    
    # code reaches here if job does is NOT already exist, so create it
    job = ProcessingJob(report_id=report_id, status="queued")
    db.add(job)
    db.commit()
    db.refresh(job)
    # set the value in redis to the actual ID
    redis_conn.set(job_key, job.id)
    
    process_report_task.delay(job.id)
    return {"job_id": job.id}

You will also need to update the celery process_report_task to delete the redis key for that report once it's completed. And add the report_id parameter to the task since it's needed for the redis key.

Note that I'm using explicit is None and is not None checks to avoid issues with False-like values.

The race condition of two jobs being created is fully avoided. The only not exactly "correct" part is when the job doesn't exist and in Redis it will temporarily have a dummy value of -1 until the job is created and updated in Redis. That means there could be a case when the 2nd request occurs, the Redis value is still -1 form the 1st request and the job has not yet been committed to the Postgres DB.

First
  |                                    
  v                                    Second
Key does not exist in Redis              |
and gets set to -1                       v
  |                                    Key exists in Redis, value -1
  v                                    don't create new job
Create Job for DB                        |
  |                                      v
  |                                    Check existing Job in DB
  |                                      |
  |                                      v
  |                                    Job not yet committed in DB, no job found
  |                                    Error!
  |
  v
Commit Job in DB
  |
  v
Update value in Redis

To address the issue of "first request's job being created but not yet committed when the second request is looking for the existing id of the job": You're already using SQLAlchemy .first() so check if the result is None and re-query until you get a result, or sleep for 0.1 seconds before each re-try, and limit total tries. Optionally, check the Job ID in Redis and instead of Postgres, which still needs retries if it's -1. But Redis get's are faster than Postgres select's (generally).

if res is None:
    # job already exists, get the current job from the DB and return that
    # but the job from the first request may not be COMMITTED to the DB yet
    while True:
        existing = db.query(ProcessingJob).(...).first()  # as above OR use Redis.GET
        if existing is not None:
            return {"job_id": existing.id}
        # maybe sleep before retrying

There are more elegant and complex ways to do this part but that's outside the scope of the question.

If the process_report_task can hang/fail and you want subsequent requests to re-create the job etc. then use the EX (expiry) Time-to-live for that key. If that's something you need, then see the Patterns section of the docs for SET:

Note: The following pattern is discouraged in favor of the Redlock algorithm which is only a bit more complex to implement, but offers better guarantees and is fault tolerant.

The command SET resource-name anystring NX EX max-lock-time is a simple way to implement a locking system with Redis.

A client can acquire the lock if the above command returns OK (or retry after some time if the command returns Nil), and remove the lock just using DEL.

The lock will be auto-released after the expire time is reached.

Q: Python match-case vs. dictionary performance internals A:

Does the compiler optimize a match-case block with literal values into a jump table or an internal hash map lookup, or does it evaluate sequentially like a traditional if-elif loop?

One way to check this is to write a benchmark. Here is a basic one:

def f3(v):
    match v:
        case 1: return 1
        case 2: return 2
        case 3: return 3
        case 4: return 4
        case 5: return 5
        case 6: return 6
        case 7: return 7
        case 8: return 8
        case 9: return 9
        case 10: return 10
        case 11: return 11
        case 12: return 12
        case 13: return 13
        case 14: return 14
        case 15: return 15
        case 16: return 16
        case 17: return 17
        case 18: return 18
        case 19: return 19
        case 20: return 20

%timeit -r 100 -n 20_000 f3(1)
%timeit -r 100 -n 20_000 f3(2)
%timeit -r 100 -n 20_000 f3(3)
%timeit -r 100 -n 20_000 f3(4)
%timeit -r 100 -n 20_000 f3(5)
%timeit -r 100 -n 20_000 f3(6)
%timeit -r 100 -n 20_000 f3(7)
%timeit -r 100 -n 20_000 f3(8)
%timeit -r 100 -n 20_000 f3(9)
%timeit -r 100 -n 20_000 f3(11)
%timeit -r 100 -n 20_000 f3(12)
%timeit -r 100 -n 20_000 f3(13)
%timeit -r 100 -n 20_000 f3(14)
%timeit -r 100 -n 20_000 f3(15)
%timeit -r 100 -n 20_000 f3(16)
%timeit -r 100 -n 20_000 f3(17)
%timeit -r 100 -n 20_000 f3(18)
%timeit -r 100 -n 20_000 f3(19)
%timeit -r 100 -n 20_000 f3(20)

Using CPython 3.12.8 on Windows, here is the timing of f3 I get based on the input value (with 100 runs and 20_000 iterations/run):

55.5 ns ± 1.32 ns per loop
69.3 ns ± 1.28 ns per loop
84.2 ns ± 1.67 ns per loop
96.8 ns ± 2.01 ns per loop
111 ns ± 0.505 ns per loop
133 ns ± 6.06 ns per loop
150 ns ± 1.73 ns per loop
165 ns ± 4.21 ns per loop
177 ns ± 2.96 ns per loop
203 ns ± 2.29 ns per loop
220 ns ± 2.91 ns per loop
232 ns ± 2.71 ns per loop
250 ns ± 3.56 ns per loop
258 ns ± 2.25 ns per loop
273 ns ± 7.28 ns per loop
288 ns ± 3.41 ns per loop
303 ns ± 2.93 ns per loop
313 ns ± 3.4 ns per loop
321 ns ± 2.74 ns per loop

We can clearly see that the time is increasing rather linearly to the input value while the same function is executed. This proves the execution time is dependent of the input value. Thus, this is a rather-strong indication that the complexity of match is O(n), especially when we look at the bytecode.

Thus, using a dictionary approach is still a good idea when there are many cases to check.

With PyPy 3.11 on Windows, the execution time seems to be also linear at first glance, but the cost of checking each case is so small that it is almost negligible. Moreover, when testing this with much more case statements, we can prove that PyPy cannot test all of them because it is faster than what the CPU can actually achieve. The thing is the PyPy JIT optimises so much the code that the whole matching statement seems mainly optimised out. Meanwhile, CPython is (mostly) an interpreter so it cannot do that (actually there is AFAIK an experimental JIT but it is AFAIK not enabled by default so far). To force PyPy not to optimise the code too much, we need to trick it or to write a more realistic benchmark. So far, PyPy seems to generate a very-fast code for the matching statement, and experimental results (with rather-small integers matches) indicate it performs a jump table optimisation, even when there are holes in the case statements. With large integers, I expect the matching code to run in O(log n) time in PyPy (because this is what mainstream compiler does in native languages like C, C++ and Rust). For even more complicated cases, I expect it to perform a linear check. Indeed, unoptimised PyPy codes generally tend to behave like CPython do.
